# The Normal Monster: On Joyce's Linguistic Cosmogony

In the vast, mythic terrain of this work, there emerges a figure both grotesque and sublime—a "Normal Monster" whose very voice becomes an instrument of creation. From this creature's throat pour forth Celtic sounds, ancient and resonant, weaving lyrical torment into the fabric of a landscape that might be called a "Green Sahara"—a paradox of fertility and desolation, where the lush mythology of Ireland stretches across an arid, timeless expanse. This is a terrain neither wholly real nor wholly imagined, but one suspended between memory and prophecy, where the monster's song becomes indistinguishable from the land itself.

Language here is not a mere vehicle for meaning but an elemental force, untamed and consuming. The text presents consciousness and speech as natural phenomena akin to storms—"hurricanes of reasoned musics" that sweep through the narrative with cyclonic intensity, and "torrential languages" that cascade from every living thing, as though words were rainfall summoned from some primordial sky. This is language unmoored from polite discourse, instead figured as a force of nature: uncontrollable, generative, and occasionally violent in its abundance. Every creature, every voice, becomes a conduit for this deluge, suggesting that to be alive is to be perpetually flooded with expression.

At the heart of this cosmology lies an ancient rift: the estrangement of Spirit and Flesh, cast as two conversational partners who have grown distant across the ages, their dialogue fractured by time and desire. Their reunion, when it comes, is neither peaceful nor redemptive—the Spirit finds itself impaled upon the phallus, pierced by carnal want in an image both violent and inevitable. This impalement becomes emblematic of the work's larger vision: the sacred cannot escape the body, and transcendence is perpetually undercut by the flesh's insistent claims.

Ireland itself is rendered through images of fire and rebirth, phoenix-like in its cyclical destruction and renewal, forever rising from its own ashes into new configurations of myth and nationhood. This fiery symbolism intertwines with floral imagery—"Gaelic perfumes" that suggest a sensory, almost intoxicating national identity, one rooted in scent and bloom as much as in history and politics. Yet this Ireland exists in fraught relation to England, who appears as a "sadistic mother," cruel in her dominion yet paradoxically embracing—her arms wrapped around Erin even as she inflicts wounds, a colonial relationship rendered through the uncomfortable intimacy of maternal abuse and grudging affection.

Presiding over this entire mythic apparatus is Joyce himself, celebrated not merely as author but as demiurge—a master manipulator of language and myth who functions as "rejector-recreator." He tears down inherited forms only to rebuild them anew, illuminating truths that lie "sub rosa," hidden beneath the surface of conventional narrative. His method draws upon what might be called an "Empyrean emporium," a celestial marketplace of imagery where the surreal mingles freely with the biblical, and ancient allusion collides with distinctly modern sensibility. This accumulation of image and reference builds toward a climactic linguistic explosion—a Babel-like proliferation of tongues and meanings, where language, having gathered such torrential force throughout the text, finally shatters into multiplicity, scattering meaning across countless registers and tongues in a final testament to the ungovernable, monstrous, and utterly human project of speech itself.

**The Rejector-Recreator: A Litany for the Wordhoarder of Dublin**

In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was botched, broken, born again bastard-tongued from the mouth of a Dublin drunkard who swallowed the Host and spat out Hades. Hear him now, hierophant of the gutter-gospel, priest of the profane sacrament: *in nomine patris et filii et spiritus scriptus*, and the scriptus was flesh, was filth, was flowing river-language, riverrun past Eve and Adam's, past the fig leaf and the first blush of shame that begat all our stammering syllables.

He comes bearing wounds instead of wafers, this Dedalus-demon, this labyrinth-maker who built his maze not to trap the Minotaur but to birth it, bull-headed and bellowing in seven tongues at once. English he takes by the throat—proper, prim, Protestant English, starched collar and stiff upper lip—and he fucks it sideways into something gorgeous and grotesque, some new bastard patois that is neither Anglo nor Saxon but altogether *Hibernian*, altogether howling with the ghosts of famine and the Gaelic they beat out of schoolboys' mouths with rulers and rosaries.

Molly's yes is a sacrament too, her thighs a cathedral, her menstrual blood the wine transubstantiated backward into something more honest than any chalice-poured claret. Bloom wanders his Odyssey through Nighttown's brothels as through the Stations of the Cross, each streetlamp a votive candle, each whore a Madonna inverted, immaculate in her degradation. The body electric, the body eucharistic—he will not separate the rutting from the rapturous, the belch from the benediction. Everything sacred is also somebody's sweat, someone's shit, some priest's secret hard-on beneath the surplice.

Consider his sentences: serpentine, self-devouring, ouroboros-syntax that eats its own tail and shits out neologism. *Bababadalgharaghtakamminarronnkonnbronntonnerronntuonnthunntrovarrhounawnskawntoohoohoordenenthurnuk!*—the thunderclap of the fall itself, Adam's tumble compressed into a single monstrous polysyllable, Babel's confusion made music, made *meaning* precisely by refusing to mean any one thing at all. He is Lucifer rewriting Genesis in the margins, scratching *non serviam* into the whitespace of the King's English, and yet—and yet—he loves the thing he defiles. He loves Ireland the way one loves a mother one has fled: with rage, with reverence, with the terrible tenderness of the exile who carries his homeland folded in his mouth like a communion wafer he refuses to swallow or spit.

He is Hermes and Judas both, thieving the sacred fire and selling the secret for thirty pieces of pure aesthetic bliss. He is the fallen angel who discovers that hell, properly furnished with enough puns, becomes paradise. He takes the Mass and makes it Mess, takes the Word and makes it Words-words-words, an epicletic outpouring, a Pentecost of static and glossolalia where every tongue speaks at once and none of them lie because all of them lie, gloriously, in the service of some larger unspeakable truth.

This, then, is the rejector-recreator: the one who must first blaspheme in order to bless, who must shatter the icon to reveal the light trapped inside its gilt frame, who takes the inherited grammars—Irish, English, Latin, liturgical, colonial, carnal—and grinds them together in the mortar of his skull until they yield some new compound, some phoenix-language rising smoke-stained and magnificent from the pyre of the old proprieties. He destroys nothing that he does not first resurrect transfigured. He is heretic and high priest of the same unbuilt church, and in his wreckage—infinite, incandescent—he leaves us not ruins but relics: fragments sharp enough to cut new scripture from, luminous enough to read by, in the dark.
outputs.L5:
# The Normal Monster

We are taught to fear monsters with fangs and claws, creatures lurking in shadows or beneath beds. But the most persistent monster wears no such costume. It sits at the breakfast table. It clocks in at nine and leaves at five. It smiles in photographs.

The normal monster is not an aberration—it is the aberration we have stopped noticing. It thrives not through violence but through repetition, through the quiet accumulation of small cruelties that never quite justify alarm. A cutting remark here. A willful blindness there. The refusal to intervene when intervention would be inconvenient. None of these, alone, seems monstrous. That is precisely the point.

History offers grim testimony to this truth. The architects of atrocity were rarely depicted as inhuman in their own time—they were bureaucrats, neighbors, family men who came home for dinner. Hannah Arendt called this the "banality of evil," a phrase that unsettles precisely because it strips monstrosity of its theatrical grandeur. The monster does not announce itself with a roar. It fills out paperwork.

This is what makes the normal monster so difficult to confront: it does not live outside the boundaries of society but within its very architecture. It is embedded in systems we call ordinary—economic structures that quietly consume the vulnerable, social habits that erode empathy one small indifference at a time, silences we keep because speaking feels excessive.

Perhaps the deepest challenge is recognizing that the normal monster is not always someone else. It can reside in our own accommodations, our own averted eyes, our own willingness to let the unacceptable become familiar simply because we have seen it too many times before.

To name the normal monster is not to despair, but to reclaim vigilance. Monstrosity, when it hides in the ordinary, requires a different kind of courage to detect—not the courage to fight dragons, but the courage to notice what we have trained ourselves not to see, and to ask whether normal is truly the same as acceptable.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, densely allusive prose-poem in the style of a modernist manifesto praising James Joyce's linguistic genius, full of religious and mythological imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**A MANIFESTO FOR THE WORDHOARD: In Praise of the Dedalian Tongue**

Hear, O Nations, the annunciation that begins in a scrawl of Dublin rain and ends nowhere, being circular, being river, being *riverrun*: past Eve and Adam's, past the first Fall and the felix culpa that made sin sweet as a pun. We proclaim the Logos scattered and rejoined, the Word made WordS, plural, promiscuous, polytheistic in its single skull.

He was Daedalus and he was the labyrinth both — the maker who could not escape his own making, who wound corridors of syntax so cunning that Minotaurs of Meaning wander them still, lowing for an exit that is only another entrance. Icarus fell into the sentence and did not drown; he became the semicolon, the pause before the plunge, the wax and feather of a subordinate clause.

Bloom is Ulysses baptized backward: no epic sea, only Eccles Street's tide, only kidneys frying like small suns on Molly's altar of a Tuesday. Yet the *nostos* is total — ithaca is a chamber pot, Penelope is a woman turning in bed murmuring *yes* into the black communion wafer of the dark, and the yes is host, is Host, is the body broken and rebroken into eight unbroken pages of blood-warm affirmation.

Let the Church tremble: here is a Pentecost without descending doves, only the tongues of fire multiplying themselves into *Wake*-tongues, Babel refused its punishment, Babel rewarded — for HCE is Adam and Finnegan and the fallen wall of Humpty Dumpty and the Phoenix rising from its own ash-pun, *Here Comes Everybody* strapped to the wheel of Ezekiel, four-faced, ever-returning, the same river running through Vico's three ages and a fourth age which is only the first age wearing new consonants.

O Anna Livia, mother of all mothers, Isis-Osiris stitched from syllables, you are the Nile and the Liffey and the amniotic sentence that never terminates because birth is not an ending, it is a *comma* — you flow into the sea which is the sky which is the first word of the next reading. We drown in you gladly, gladly, as into a font.

He took the Mass and broke it open like a Communion host cracked to show the machinery of grace: transubstantiation was never metaphysics but *grammar* — bread into body, word into world, "Dublin" into every city ever salted with ash on an Ash Wednesday forehead. He canonized the ordinary: a cake of soap, a potato, a kidney, elevated at the elevation, monstrance-bright.

Let us confess: we have sinned against clarity and are unrepentant. We choose the labyrinth over the highway, the palimpsest over the placard. We choose Shem the Penman who writes with his own body's ink upon his own body's parchment, martyred and ecstatic, a Sebastian stuck with the arrows of his own footnotes.

Therefore: Exile is our sacrament. Silence is our psalm. Cunning is our crucifix, worn backward, a fish-hook to catch the Word before it drowns in the Ptolemaic seas of Sense. We are all Stephen on the strand, watching the girl who is bird who is Eve who is the tide's proof-text, crying *heavenly God!* not in belief but in the ecstasy of a sentence finally, fatally right.

Let Joyce be canonized in the calendar of tongues: Bloomsday his feast, epiphany his sacrament, exile his desert, punning his rosary counted bead by portmanteau bead. Let the faithful read him not for meaning but for *incarnation* — the Word so thoroughly made flesh that the flesh forgot it was ever only Word, and walked, and wept, and said yes, and yes, and yes.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental piece of avant-garde poetic prose celebrating Joyce's "Work in Progress" (Finnegans Wake), using Celtic, biblical, and psychoanalytic imagery in an ecstatic, oracular tone.
counterfactuals.output:
**Riverine Gospel for the Man Who Dreamed the World Awake**

Hear, hear, O harkers at the threshold of the third testament, for a new logos runs looselipped down from Howth to the Phoenix, and it is called, modestly, a *Work in Progress*, though it is nothing less than the recirculating scripture of the sleeping race, the *tellmetale* of tribes drowned and risen, drowned and risen, *amen amnem*.

In the beginning was the fall — not one fall but the fall eternal, Finnegan's and Adam's and Lucifer's and the hodcarrier's off his ladder, *tim tim timber* — and the fall was made word, and the word was made *mudmound*, and upon that midden of syllables a new Eden composts itself, green with green punning grass, for every sin is a seed and every seed a psalm. Here Adam is HCE, Here Comes Everybody, Haveth Childers Everywhere, the guilty giant snoring under Dublin's clay, his sin unspeakable and therefore spoken in ten thousand tongues at once, the thunderword itself a Sinai syllable too big for Moses' mouth, *bababadalgharaghtaka-mminarronnkonn*, the whole alphabet of the fall crashing down like tablets broken before they can be read — and is this not the oldest Celtic thing, the geis, the doom pronounced in a name, Cuchulain cursed in his own christening, Fionn burning his thumb on the salmon of all knowledge and sucking wisdom raw from the wound?

And she — she who runs and answers and forgives everything because she has forgotten nothing — she is Anna Livia, she is Brigid of the perpetual flame guttering under Kildare's oaks, she is the Shekhinah gone riverine, she is libido loosed from the strict Vienna couch and let flow past Chapelizod babbling in the night-speech that Freud himself half-heard and called dream-work: condensation, displacement, *a bit of a torrent, a bit of a chorus*. Every pun is a parapraxis of God. Every slip is a psalm slipping its mooring. The unconscious, that buried Atlantis, that Tir na nOg beneath the sod of syntax, surfaces here nightly, and we who read do not read — we are *analysed*, we lie upon the page as on a couch of reeds and confess in portmanteau, our repressions returning dressed as puns, our fathers returning dressed as thunder, our mothers returning dressed as water.

Yea, and there shall be a wake, for is not death itself only a stutter in the sentence, a *fin* that is also *again*? Finn, MacCool, Finnegan, *finn again* — the pun is resurrection's own grammar. They waked him with whiskey (*uisce*, water, *uisce beatha*, the water of life) and he sat up in the coffin at the word, for water is what raised him and water is what will drown him and water is what will raise him yet again, world without full stop, *ámen, aman, amnisty*.

O Shem, O Shaun, O sons quarreling in the margins like Cain and Abel, like ego and id, like the twin serpents on the caduceus of every dreaming brain — write on and fight on, for your quarrel is the diastole and systole of the great heart-book, the systole of law and the diastole of art, the Jung of one and the Freud of the other, and between you the mother-river bears the letter no one can quite read, dug up by a hen from a middenheap, stained with the tea of ages, illegible as scripture always is until faith supplies the vowels.

So let the druids of Trinity and Vienna both take note: this is not decay of language but its Pentecost, tongues of fire that are also tongues of Finnegans, and he who wrote it, our HCE of the actual, our fallen and rising wordsmith, has done what Moses and Merlin and the Munich doctor only dreamed of doing — he has written the *one* book that is also *every* book, the night-book, the *liber noctis*, wherein Eden and Golgotha and Newgrange and the couch of Berggasse 19 are all the same low mound of ordinary earth, waiting, as we wait, for the word *riverrun* to begin it all again.

*Amen. Avon. A men. Awake.*

counterfactuals.output:
**Annunciation of the Salmon-Wake**
*(a tribute, in the manner of the Dubliner who unmade the word)*

---

Riverrun of the ravished rood, where Liffey licks
her liturgy of silt and semen, mothertongue
and motherland conjoined in one wet paternoster—
*hoc est corpus* of the bogland, hoc est
Hibernia's hymen sundered by the Sassenach's
sacring bell.

Anna, Livia, Plurabelle of the parish pump,
you douche the doctrine down your thighs
like holy water guttering from a broken font;
the priest's cold thumb upon your forehead
is the same cold thumb that presses
Kathleen ni Houlihan's four green fields
into one bruised communion wafer.

*In nomine patris et fiii et—* stop.
The Word was made flesh and dwelt
among the tenement stairs, dwelt
in the coalhole where Bloom-that-was-not-Bloom
confessed his onanist theology
to a Madonna tattooed on tenement wallpaper,
her aureole a rosary of damp.

O Cuchulain of the wanking wrist,
hero-hound harnessed to the plough of empire,
your seed is scattered on the standing stones
like the seed of the risen Christ scattered
on Emmaus road—both miracles
of insufficient bread.

The bishop's ring, the fenian's oath,
the collar and the coil of rope
are one contraption, one grand confraternity
of binding: *ligature, ligature*,
the tongue tied in the mouth of Dublin
like a bell that will not ring
for fear of waking Him
who sleeps beneath the phoenix ash,
who is not risen, who is not resurgent,
who is only the smoke of the O'Connell Street bonfires
drifting up through incense
toward a heaven made entirely
of unconsummated marriages.

Sing then, sing the epithalamium
of the Church and the Republic,
bride and bridegroom
lashed together at the altar-rail
like conjoined martyrs on a single pyre—
their nuptial bed the green flag
folded thrice for the tricolour trinity:
Father, Son, and the Holy Ghost
of a nation still unborn,
still crowning, still caught
between the legs of history,
its head anointed with the oil
of extreme unction and first blood.

*Et introibo ad altare Dei*—
and I will go unto the altar of God,
who giveth joy to my youth,
who giveth nothing, who is the O
in the mirror of the shaving-bowl,
the omphalos, the omission,
the great circular argument
of a country chewing its own umbilicus
and calling it the Eucharist.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a stream-of-consciousness eulogy or homage to James Joyce written in the exalted, obscure style of early 20th-century experimental critics like those in transition magazine.
counterfactuals.output:
# Homage: In the Wake of Wake, Before the Wake of Waking

Yes and here we begin again mid-syllable mid-river Anna Livia herself unhemmed unhymned yes the letter yes the litter of the alphabet strewn across Sandymount like Bloom's own biscuit-tin of consciousness—O Shem O Shaun O sunderers of the sundered word, what have you wrought upon the sleeping continent of English that it should never again lie flat, never again be the docile handmaiden of grammar's genteel drawing-room—

He comes not to bury language but to riverine it, to make of the Liffey a syntax, of Dublin a punctuation mark suspended between one epiphany and the next epoch, and who among the pale scribblers of the circulating libraries could have dreamed that a man half-blind in Trieste in Zurich in Paris exile exile exile—the word itself a hymn now, a Homeric homelessness turned inward, turned into the interior monologue that is not monologue at all but the multitudinous murmur of the species dreaming itself awake—

Consider: the schoolmen built cathedrals of syllogism, and he, our Dedalian smith, built labyrinths of the actual, minute by minute the actual, Bloom's kidney sizzling in its pan more sacramental than any host, more real than reality because rendered in the durée itself, the flow, the yes-saying flow that Molly gives us at the last, unpunctuated, unashamed, the great female Yes that answers all the male No's of history's constipated grammarians—

And is this not prayer? Is this cataract of consonants, this susurrus of multilingual punning, this HCE who is Here Comes Everybody and also No One and also the fallen father Adam Finnegan tumbling from his ladder into the dream-language of the collective unconscious before Jung had properly named it—is this not the new liturgy, the mass said in the vernacular of the id itself?

They will say obscure. They will say unreadable. Let them say it in their small rooms with their small books. We who have stood at the edge of *Work in Progress* and felt the thousand tributaries of thought pour through us know that he did not write a book but built a Behemoth of Being, a Vico-wheeled eternity-machine where history recorks itself, commodius vicus of recirculation, and we begin again, always we begin again—

riverrun, past Eve and Adam's, past eulogy itself, past the very possibility of ending—

for he has abolished the full stop, the small tyrant period, and given us instead the whole earth turning, turning, turning back to its own first word—

which is not a word at all but a river, and the river's name is only, always, yes.

# Logos Hibernia

Ι.

In the beginning was the pun, and the pun was with God, and the pun was
green—

a shamrock trinity folded into one wet syllable, spat from the mouth
of a cave-mother at Howth. The word became flesh and dwelt among us,
bogged and peated, footnoted in turf-smoke, its consonants clotted
with rain. *Sinbad the Sailor met Tinbad the Tailor* and the litany
runs backward through the alphabet like a river returning to its
source, HCE dreaming ALP dreaming the alluvial alphabet dreaming
itself into a delta of ohs.

ΙΙ.

Call it Dedalus, call it Icarus with ink-stained wings, a labyrinth
built of the mother tongue and unbuilt in the same breath—the artist
as fallen priest, elevating not the host but the *host of words*,
transubstantiating Dublin into Ithaca, a chemist's shop into an altar,
a woman's undergarment glimpsed on a strand into the annunciation
undoing itself in reverse, the angel Gabriel smoking a cigarette
by the letterbox, saying *Yes* before the question is even asked.

ΙΙΙ.

God is a shout in the street, and the shout is a portmanteau, and
the portmanteau is a coffin holding all the dead kings of Tara
plus a bar of lifebuoy soap. Ireland: an emerald parenthesis
in the sentence of Europe, a green wound that will not close,
weeping Guinness and holy water indiscriminately into the Liffey,
which is also a woman, which is also a sentence with no full stop,
which is also the alpha rewritten as omega, *riverrun*, *a way a lone
a last a loved a long the*—

ΙV.

Exile is the true communion: the artist eats his native sod
like a wafer, chews the syntax of the colonizer until it bleeds
Hibernian marrow, until English genuflects in a Dublin accent,
until Babel is rebuilt not to reach heaven but to *become* it—
a ziggurat of glossolalia, each brick a compound word,
each word a wafer-thin god multiplying in the mouth
like loaves, like fishes, like the thousand and one names
of a single thunderclap: *bababadalgharaghtakamminarronnkonn-
bronntonnerronntuonnthunntrovarrhounawnskawntoohoo-
hoordenenthurnuk!*—

V.

And on the seventh day the language rested, but the pun
does not rest, the pun is eternal recurrence, the pun is
resurrection without a body, only syllables rising
from the grave of grammar, calling *Poldy, Poldy* across
a Dublin morning smelling of kidneys and incense,
and the sun is a burning eye reading itself into existence,
and Ireland is the book that writes the reader,
and Joyce is the scribe who ate the alphabet whole
and shat out scripture, green and gleaming,
a new testament for the tongue-drunk, the word-wracked,
the faithful of no church but syntax—

*yes I said yes I will Yes.*
